2.11.0: v2.11.0 puts MailVault in nine languages — English, Spanish, French, Italian, German, Brazilian Portuguese, Japanese, Korean and Simplified Chinese — across every screen, the menu bar, the tray, its notifications and the errors it reports, with dates and times following the language you chose rather than the one your computer is set to. Pick one in Settings and it changes as you watch. The translations ship inside the app, so choosing one tells nobody anything. It also lets a message leave MailVault without losing what made it evidence. Any message, or a whole conversation, can now be saved as a PNG of exactly what you were reading, or as one self-contained HTML file that folds every message in the thread behind a line giving its date and sender — no JavaScript, no fonts to fetch, no server that has to still be alive. Remote images are pulled in during the export and written into the file itself, so it still reads years later with the network unplugged, and every file says underneath which account and folder it came from, each message's identifier, and how many remote images were mirrored, refused, or dropped for being tracking pixels. Nothing that can execute survives the export. That is a Premium feature; without a subscription the same button renders three real samples on the spot, which you can open or save. MailVault also now tells everyone, free and forever, when an email is watching them: an eye beside the subject names the company behind the hidden pixel and the exact address it would have called, and with a subscription the beacon is taken out before the message is drawn, so the sender is told nothing at all. On Linux, spellcheck now says which dictionary to install instead of looking like a button that does not work, and on macOS the red underlines finally appear — the toolbar switch has been there since 2.10.4 with nothing behind it. An open message drops the second, quieter claim about where it lives, so the band at the top is its one statement, and “Report a bug” now takes feature requests too. A message that refused to open with “connection lost” now opens on the first try: MailVault noticed a reused server connection had died under it only after handing you the error. This release is also the first one that introduces itself: a new install now opens on a short tour that asks which of the nine languages to use, says what MailVault does with a mailbox and where the password goes, lets you add one there and then — or skip it and carry on — and asks how the app should look against a real message list that changes as you pick, while the first mailbox is already being fetched behind it. Settings now says what a subscription buys instead of only what it costs: Billing lists every Premium feature above the plan card, each linking into the screen it belongs to, and Help carries the same gallery and a link to the FAQ in your language. The FAQ itself is now six pages behind a searchable hub rather than one long scroll. And the auto-cleanup rules that archive or delete old mail have never once run: the settings screen and the engine disagreed about how a rule is written down, so every rule anyone ever made sat there doing nothing. That is fixed — and because a dormant rule waking up unannounced would be worse than the bug, every stored rule has been switched off with a notice saying why. Turning one back on is one toggle, and it is yours to make.
2.10.4: v2.10.4 makes the gold “your only copy” mark mean what it says: MailVault now asks your mail server whether an archived message still exists in any folder on it, and only turns the row gold when every folder has answered and none of them has it. The mark also stops falling off messages after an archive and in search results, a reply now leaves from the mailbox you were reading rather than whichever account sent last, a backup that saved 788 of 789 messages reports itself as partial instead of failed, MailVault says so plainly when Premium stops applying to this computer, and the compose toolbar can turn spellcheck off and keep it off. Automatic backups now require a subscription: the master switch above the per-account ones was never gated, so one flip on a free install backed up every account and announced each run — manual backups stay free. And the small dot that means your backup drive holds a copy stops borrowing the vault's own green, stops disagreeing with the message you have open, stops answering for a message in Sent with an unrelated inbox message's number, and says nothing at all when you have never set up a backup drive. “Report a bug” now asks where the report should land — a public thread in the project’s Bug Reports discussions, or the same email as before — and a second button under it opens a ready-written note for passing MailVault on to someone. An archived “only copy” message also stops painting its whole row gold: the symbol, the label and the band still say it, and the row answers the pointer like every other row. And the whole app stops sliding out of its own window: it fills the window exactly, so there was nothing to scroll, yet a firm flick on the trackpad dragged every pane downwards with no scrollbar to pull them back.
2.10.3: v2.10.3 is a fix release, and the fixes are about one thing: MailVault filing your mail under numbers that only ever meant something to the server that issued them. Move a domain to a new mail host and those numbers get handed to different messages — so a message in a conversation showed its own subject line where its text should have been, "View Source" could hand you a different message entirely, and every backup quietly undid MailVault's own repair of the archive by copying the outdated copies back in. It also stops a narrow window from pushing the message you clicked below the bottom edge, brings the hidden Settings tabs back onto the screen, and gives a screen reader a running commentary on bulk archive and delete.
